The ADR says a clan 'carries a founding bloodline ... and reads that bloodline's purity on a member as a STANDING MULTIPLIER, never as a stat the clan grants. This is the hinge that connects the three systems'. MEASURED: ClanGate.standing_of (clan/clan_gate.gd:156) returns the raw integer from the ledger; its one caller inside the module is _standing_at_least (clan_gate.gd:194), which compares it to a threshold. The ONLY reader of BloodlineApi.purity_of anywhere in modules/clan is ClanGate.admission_unmet (clan_gate.gd:100), and that is a THRESHOLD COMPARISON at the door, not a multiplier on standing. ClanApi.summary:220 publishes founding_purity as a display value. So purity in the clan module is: a gate at admission, and a number on a screen. The multiplier the ADR, ClanApi's own module docstring (api.gd:19), and ClanDef's field docs (clan_def.gd:18, :45) all describe does not exist. This matters more than a missing feature because the ADRs use it as the PROOF the three modules are connected - 'a member of a high-standing clan with a diluted bloodline is a legitimate and interesting character: the clan recognises them, the lineage does not empower them. That gap is the point.' Without the multiplier, a high-standing member of a diluted line is indistinguishable from any other member, and the interesting character the ADR describes cannot be built. It is also not observable: the sentence 'the clan grants recognition and never power' is preserved (correctly - the fix must stay a PERCENT at most, and per ADR 0084 never a FLAT), so nothing goes red today and this is invisible to the suite. NEXT STEP: decide whether the multiplier is wanted and in what direction. Standing x purity would make a weak lineage actively COST recognition, which is the opposite of what the ADR describes - so the likely correct reading is that the bloodline should multiply what the member's own lineage is WORTH (a recognition coefficient surfaced to the social layer), not that it should scale a clan integer. Whichever it is, it needs its own ADR because it makes clan contribute to a stat surface, and ADR 0084 plus rules.MAX_FACADE_PUBLIC_METHODS (clan is at the twelve-method cap) both constrain the shape.

title: act_pickup has no stale-reward guard while act_take_all has one: the asymmetry behind 224 pending
source: read 2026-10-04 while building the boot probe's refusal discriminator
next: THE ASYMMETRY, in game/src/ui/screens/loot_encounter.gd, which is the strongest lead yet on BL-0697 (224 pending, nothing collected). act_take_all(encounter_id) at :225-236 DOES guard a stale row: it reads shown := _reward_list.encounter_id() and, at :232-233, returns _reject('stale_reward') when the signal names a reward that is not the one on screen. Its own docstring at :220-224 states the rule: this screen lists exactly one reward, so a signal naming a DIFFERENT one means the button belongs to a reward no longer on screen, and taking from a reward the player cannot see is worse than refusing. act_pickup(drop_id) at :156-166 has NO such guard. It reads encounter_id from _reward_list.encounter_id() and calls pickup with it, but never checks that the drop being pressed belongs to that listed reward. WHY THAT PRODUCES OUR SYMPTOM. game/tools/boot_probe.gd:567-570 resolves the first node named DropAction inside the reward list and emits pressed on it; the probe re-resolves the SCREEN each pass but not the ROW, so a pooled row can survive a repaint and outlive the reward it was built for. LootState.pickup then returns ERR_UNKNOWN_DROP (game/src/modules/loot/loot_state.gd:419-427) - a refusal the player cannot act on - and pending_drops stays flat, which is exactly 'taking a drop left 224 of 224 pending'. I CONFIRM pending is a real number, not an artefact: LootRewards.view (loot_rewards.gd:172-186) counts a drop pending when it is neither claimed nor stashed, so genuinely unclaimed drops do appear. What is unexplained is only why no press ever succeeds. WHAT I HAVE ALREADY DONE so the next run measures instead of guessing. game/tools/boot_probe.gd now records the refusal the screen published for EACH press (a refusals array, bounded by the same MAX_DROPS_PER_REWARD as the walk), and the stuck-path verdict embeds them: 'taking a drop left N of N pending; nothing was collected; each press published: <reasons>'. One run therefore separates ERR_UNKNOWN_DROP from ERR_CLAIM_SPENT / ERR_UNKNOWN_REWARD / ERR_DROP_CLAIMED / ERR_DROP_STASHED / ERR_WORLD_FULL / ERR_INVENTORY_FULL. The helper reads only summary() keys the screen already publishes (last_reason / last_ok) and returns the token 'no_outcome_reported' when it publishes neither - deliberately NOT a default of success, because a probe that invents a pass is the one answer this must rule out. OWNERSHIP: game/tools/boot_probe.gd is ROOT's and mine; game/src/ui/screens/loot_encounter.gd belongs to the running BL-0699 agent, so I did NOT edit it. If that agent publishes last_reason/last_ok from act_pickup, my probe reads it with no further change on my side. STATUS: hypothesis, NOT proven. The asymmetry is real in the code; that it is THE cause of 224 pending is unverified until a run prints the reasons.

title: tools boot leaks 213 ObjectDB instances and 86 resources at exit
source: observed 2026-10-04 in build/BOOTD.txt, from the probe's own run
next: NARROWED, 2026-10-04, by reading rather than guessing. game/tools/boot_probe.gd instantiates EXACTLY ONE node in its whole life: 'var app := packed.instantiate()' at boot_probe.gd:120, and it frees it correctly at :228-229 with 'root.remove_child(app)' then 'app.free()' - detach before free, which is the order AGENTS.md requires because the engine holds the parent pointer. A grep for free() / remove_child / instantiate across the file returns only those three sites plus two docstring mentions (lines 47 and one other). So the 213 leaked ObjectDB instances are NOT the mounted app subtree, and the sweep does not leak a node per attempt - which is the shape I feared, because a leak scaling with MAX_SWEEP_CELLS (160) would scale with the work the gate asked for. WHAT REMAINS AS THE LIKELY SOURCE, stated as a hypothesis and NOT as a finding. The probe runs as '-s res://tools/boot_probe.gd', i.e. a SceneTree script that calls quit() rather than exiting through the engine's normal shutdown. Autoloads, their owned resources, and anything they hold are therefore never released, and Godot reports exactly this as 'N ObjectDB instances were leaked at exit'. Under that reading the count is a per-run constant that reflects the project's singletons, not a defect in the probe, and it would appear identically for any '-s' script in this project. WHY IT IS STILL WORTH AN ENTRY rather than being dismissed. I have NOT proven that reading: proving it needs a --verbose run to name the leaked classes, and I do not have that output (build/logs/*bootprobe.log did not exist for the run I measured). So this entry records the eliminated candidate, the surviving hypothesis, and the one command that settles it. If --verbose names only autoload-owned classes, close this as not-a-defect and say so here; if it names a Control or a screen from game/src, it is a real leak in shipped code and belongs to whoever owns that class. WHAT I DID NOT DO, deliberately: reproduce the leak with a loop, raise an engine threshold, or suppress the warning. AGENTS.md is explicit that reproducing a runaway to diagnose it spends the user's disk, RAM and time to re-learn what the ceiling already reported.

next: CORRECTS MY OWN DUPLICATE, and the correction is the finding. I filed this asserting a corpus dilution gap. That is BL-0625's retracted claim: gear is widely available, so 'tables bury gear' is not a defect. WHAT IS NEW HERE IS THE DENOMINATOR BL-0625 LACKED. Measured over the LOWEST tier of each of the 160 authored encounters (the band a starter hero actually enters), 331 distinct tables are reachable and 281 of them carry at least one wearable entry, so the OBTAINABLE half is genuinely yes. But 246 of those 331 (74%) put the wearable share below 10% per single roll, because every entry carries weight=1.0 across tables of 2-45 entries: loot_F5_ascension_warden 0/2, loot_ember_hound_t1 0/3, loot_amulet_iron_sage 1/25. No entry-band table is 100% gear. That is what makes the boot gate's equip half red, and it is a real fact about per-roll dilution even though it is not a content gap. THE RUN THAT PROVED IT, and its ids are the value here: build/BOOTF.txt at commit 2c0924cc reads 'none of the 2 drop(s) this fight paid can be worn (I50_earth_geyser_aged, Z27_immortal_augustinian_label); a starter equips: armor_iron_helm'. Both named ids are content, not equipment - I50_earth_geyser_aged is category=consumable subcategory=powder (game/data/items/consumable/), Z27_immortal_augustinian_label is category=misc subcategory=token (game/data/items/misc/). So the control is exonerated (a starter equips, so %EquipButton works and the bag row selects) and the drops are simply unwearable. WHICH TABLES PAID THEM: I50_earth_geyser_aged is entry 11 of loot_amulet_iron_sage, Z27_immortal_augustinian_label is in loot_d1_iron_sage_adept. Both are the tier-1 Gate bosses of loot_amulet_iron_sage_domain, and loot_amulet_iron_sage carries exactly one wearable entry (armor_boar_hide) among 21 items plus 4 pool tables. Two equal-weight rolls out of 25 landing on two non-gear entries is unremarkable: P is about 92%. NEXT STEP: this is a PROBE defect and belongs with BL-0725/BL-0369, not with content. The sweep must either walk a table the entry band reaches with high gear share (loot_ember_warden_t1 is 4/22 and is exactly the table BL-0625 named) or stop asserting anything about the corpus from a slice. Do NOT widen MAX_EQUIP_HUNTS to paper over it: at ~4-8% per fight, 24 hunts reaches a 96% event only in expectation, and a gate that passes 96% of the time is not a gate. The honest fix is to fight a table authored to pay gear, and to keep the per-roll shares above as the number that says why.

title: tools boot is not hermetic: it restores user://save/primary.json, so the gate's verdict depends on whichever run touched the user's profile last
source: root 2026-10-04, ItemWorkbenchApp._ready:152 + SavePaths.PRIMARY (save/save_paths.gd:25), reached while correcting BL-0736
next: THIS INVALIDATES GATE MEASUREMENTS TAKEN ACROSS RUNS, including some of my own, and it should be settled before any more of them are believed. THE MECHANISM, read from code not inferred: ItemWorkbenchApp._ready calls restore_actor() and only calls _build_actor() when that returns not-ok (game/src/app/item_workbench_app.gd:152). restore_actor reaches SaveApi.restore, which reads SavePaths.PRIMARY = user://save/primary.json (game/src/modules/save/save_paths.gd:25). That path is user://, so it resolves to %APPDATA%/Godot/app_userdata/Chaos World/save/primary.json - OUTSIDE the repository, in the user's profile, and it is shared by every task that boots the app (tools boot, tools run, tools ui). So a run's starting actor, bag, equipment and outstanding loot payloads are whatever the last run left behind. WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A TIDYNESS COMPLAINT: a gate step whose verdict depends on untracked external state is not reproducible, and every 'the sweep degraded', 'the bag was full', 'hunts 1' and 'rows_at_boot 0' observation I or a peer has recorded is suspect to exactly the degree that the previous run differed. I hit this myself: I attributed a full 24-row bag to nine fights (BL-0736) and a peer had measured a restored save carrying 113 payloads and bag 23/24, which fills the bag with no fight at all. CONFIRMED SHAPE OF THE INSTABILITY, not speculation: at 09:08 the save directory did not exist and the same command reported rows_at_boot 0; at 09:19 it still did not exist and the same command reported rows_at_boot 4. The file's presence is not under the repo's control and is not cleaned by anything in tools/. NEXT STEP, and the cheap fix is first: tools/godot.py should point --user-data-dir (or the equivalent) at a build/ path the runner owns, so every gate run starts from a state the runner controls and can delete. That is one argument in one launcher, it needs no gameplay change, and it makes every other measurement in this file trustworthy. Only after that should the poison itself be investigated - 113 outstanding payloads that can never be shed is a separate defect, and BL-0699's agent recorded that the claim backlog is monotone. Do NOT 'fix' this by deleting the user's save from a task: that is a destructive action on state outside the repo, and the right answer is to stop reading it at all.

title: A full bag advertises reclaim, but reclaim needs the free space the overflow refused: the recovery is closed in the state that needs it
source: root 2026-10-04, read from LootState.reclaim (loot_state.gd:514-546), LootState.pickup overflow (:447) and ItemsApi's twelve verbs
next:
READ FROM CODE, NOT OBSERVED IN A RUN, and the distinction matters because it is a structural claim rather than a measurement.

THE DEADLOCK. A pickup refused by a full bag parks the drop in the bounded world container and the panel tells the player "the drop is in the world and can be reclaimed". That sentence promises a recovery. The recovery cannot run in the state that needs it. LootState.reclaim (game/src/modules/loot/loot_state.gd:514) takes the inventory and checks `if not LootRewards.fits(drop, inventory, realized) or LootRewards.deliver(drop, inventory) > 0` before returning ERR_INVENTORY_FULL and leaving the drop stashed. So reclaim needs exactly the free space that the overflow refused to consume. The two paths are symmetric refusals of the same precondition, which means a full bag parks a drop it can never recover until something else frees a slot.

WHAT ELSE CAN FREE A SLOT, and this is the part that decides whether it is a deadlock or a pressure valve. The bag is Inventory's authored default of 24 slots (inventory.gd:19), and ItemsApi exposes twelve verbs (attach, inventory, equipment, craft, has_item, consume_item, equip_item, unequip_to_inventory, generate, use_item, serialize, deserialize). There is no sell and no discard. The only verbs that reduce a stack are consume_item, use_item and unequip_to_inventory, and the first two DESTROY the item. So the escape from a full bag is to throw something away, and the only way to throw something away that the game offers is to consume or use it - which for a piece of gear destroys it rather than banking it. That is a real player-facing constraint and it is authored somewhere; whether 24 is the intended number is not a question this entry can answer from a log line.

WHY IT IS WORTH NAMING SEPARATELY FROM BL-0736. That entry measures WHEN the bag fills (nine fights, rows_at_boot 4 to rows_now 24). This entry is about what a full bag does to the recovery the UI advertises, which is a FAILURE REACHABLE and WIRED OUT question: the wording promises a path and the path is closed in exactly the circumstance the player is in. Criterion 7 asks for the concrete input state that triggers each refusal branch, and the honest answer for reclaim is "a full bag", which is also the state that produced the stash.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. I did not observe a player being stuck; I read that the guard exists and is symmetric. A run would confirm the wording is shown and the reclaim then refuses, but the lock is held and a structural read is the stronger evidence anyway - it holds regardless of RNG. Do NOT 'fix' this by raising WORLD_DROP_CAPACITY or the bag size without an authored decision on inventory pressure: both change how much loot a session holds, which is a balance decision, and raising the world cap makes the unrecoverable stash larger rather than recoverable.

title: UNADOPTED: a background agent left an unexecuted loot validator in the tree that contradicts an independent measurement and reds 4 cases
source: root 2026-10-04, agent report 'my code has NEVER been executed' plus tools test --suite payable_tables
next:
HARD CONSTRAINT ADDED, AND IT MAKES THE DECISION EASIER. The unadopted work pushes game/src/modules/loot/loot_content.gd over the gdlint max-public-methods cap of 20. Measured: HEAD declares 18 public methods; the working tree declares 24. The breach is the agent's own six - provide_table, bound_table_ids, band_bound_tables, unbanded_tables, band_reachable_item_ids and forget_boss - plus two private helpers that do not count against the cap. So adopting the validator as written means shipping a lint failure in a gate, which is not a judgement call about whether the arithmetic is sound: the shape does not fit.

That is the second independent reason not to adopt it as-is, and it changes what the next owner should do. The capability is right - a table no defeat can resolve ships items no player can obtain - but six new public query methods on a content singleton is the wrong shape for it. The same answers are available from what already exists: band_bound_tables is a closure over bound_table_ids, and the runtime resolver already walks that closure in loot_resolver.gd. So the honest options are to put the scope check in the VALIDATOR rather than on the content singleton (loot_validator.gd is where a check belongs and adding to it costs no public surface), or to fold the queries into one entry point that returns the answer rather than six that each return a piece of it.

This also settles the isolation question from a different angle: if the queries move into the validator, they take a LootContent as a parameter instead of reaching for the shared singleton, and the pollution that made the agent read 8 tables where there are 0 stops being possible by construction rather than by convention. One change fixes the cap breach, the pollution, and the unverified-code problem together, which is the strongest argument for that shape over keeping the six methods.

Verified by count rather than by reading the lint line: 18 in HEAD, 24 in the working tree, cap 20. All 10 lint errors currently in the tree are in files this entry does not own except this one.

title: LootContent.instance() is a static singleton that survives between suites, so any corpus-scanning test sees another suite's injected fixtures
source: root 2026-10-04, found resolving BL-0758's 0-versus-8 disagreement: probe_projected_loot_bear belongs to test_loot_encounter.gd:655, not to the suite that found it
next:
TWO WRITERS, FIVE READERS, ONE PROCESS. LootContent.instance() memoises into static var shared (game/src/modules/loot/loot_content.gd), and the headless runner drives every suite in one process, so anything a suite injects is still there for the next one. Two suites WRITE to it: test_loot_resolver.gd:431 calls LootContent.instance().provide(def.id, def), and test_loot_boss_striking_profile.gd:89 calls provide_boss on the singleton (that one does save and restore the prior value at :458, so it is the better-behaved of the two). Five suites READ the whole corpus through it - test_loot_content.gd, test_loot_domain_reachability.gd, test_loot_encounter.gd, test_loot_payable_tables.gd, test_loot_unique_routes - plus a dozen call sites across game/tests/acquisition/. The corpus answer any of them gets therefore depends on which suites ran first, which makes the suite order part of the contract without anything stating it.

THE EVIDENCE IS A REAL MISCOUNT, not a theoretical one. A validator scanning the corpus through the singleton reported 8 unpayable tables; a scan of the authored .tres text found 0. The difference was one of those 8 being probe_projected_loot_bear, a fixture belonging to test_loot_encounter.gd:655 - another suite's test furniture, reported as shipped content. The count was small rather than large precisely because it was furniture: a real corpus gap would have been in the hundreds. That is BL-0758.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR THE AUDIT RATHER THAN FOR THIS ONE SUITE. The acquisition suites in game/tests/acquisition/ are the evidence for OBTAINABLE, and they all read the shared singleton. A count they produce is only as trustworthy as the isolation around it, and today nothing enforces that. This is the same defect as BL-0743 one layer down - a gate whose verdict depends on untracked state - except here the untracked state is another test's leftovers rather than a file in the user's profile.

THE FIX, and the cheap half first. Any suite that scans the corpus should build its own LootContent.new() rather than call instance(); test_loot_domain_reachability.gd:31-34 and test_loot_payable_tables.gd:35-40 already do exactly that, with a comment naming instance() as the thing being avoided, so the pattern and its rationale are both already in the tree. What is missing is anything stopping the other five. A guard test that asserts no suite calls a mutating provide on the singleton, or that the singleton's table count is unchanged across a suite boundary, would make the isolation enforced instead of conventional - and by the INC-0016 rule it has to be mutation-proven to go red before it counts.

DO NOT fix this by clearing the singleton between suites. That hides real order dependence rather than removing it, and it would let a genuine cross-suite dependency keep passing. Make each scanner own its corpus.

title: The rate guard has one enforcement point and it is in contracts; a core.is_rate(id) aggregator would let module-owned sets reach both gates without restating them
next: NOT FIXED, NEEDS A core/ CHANGE AND ITS OWN ADR. ADR 0171 had to declare nine module-owned ids as consts in game/src/contracts/stat.gd because that is the only file tools/data.py:2085 (_resolve_rate_stats) and modules/status/status_def.gd:372 can resolve a name against. So every module that invents a rate now has to be registered by hand in another module's contract, and the only thing stopping that drifting is the new guard (game/tests/contracts/test_rate_stats_registration.gd), which fails only when the rename is observable. The structural fix is one core function: ActorStats.is_rate(id) -> bool that unions each module's PUBLISHED rate set (CombatStats.RATE_IDS already exists in the right shape; MindStats has no equivalent), and both gates call that instead of the array. Then contracts/stat.gd carries only core's own ids and ADR 0068's 'do not add dynamic ids to RATE_STATS' is satisfiable again.

title: data options coverage proves a consumer EXISTS, never that a modifier has an EFFECT, and a PERCENT on a zero-baseline stat passes it and grants nothing
source: BL-0675 fix, measured 2026-10-04; confirms BL-0676's premise
next: STILL TRUE, NOT FIXED, NOT CLOSED BY BL-0675. Confirmed by reading tools/check.py:82 (runs data options coverage --fail-on error) and tools/options.py:581-626 (_audit): neither checks a modifier's op against the target's BASELINE, only against the option's own unit field. Coverage classifies a target as core/provider/element/property/resource and mind_avoidance passes as 'provider'. So a PERCENT on any id whose baseline is identically zero still passes the gate and still evaluates to (0.0 + 0.0) * (1 + p) = 0.0 (core/actor_stats.gd:181-196). title: CONTRACT: three assertions in test_quest_acquisition.gd encode the UNSHIPPED quest contract and must be inverted when the delivery edge lands
source: WAVE 5 audit, found 2026-10-04 before the flag flip
next:
FOUND BEFORE IT BIT, and it is a contract change with three named tests on the other side of it. Recording it here so the flag flip cannot land without someone reading this.

game/tests/acquisition/test_quest_acquisition.gd asserts the CURRENT, un-delivering behaviour in three places, and all three go red the moment quest stops being unshipped:

  1. test_the_runtime_itself_reports_the_quest_source_kind_as_unshipped (line 170) asserts `ItemSources.is_shipped(ItemSources.KIND_QUEST)` is FALSE and that KIND_QUEST is in `unshipped_kind_ids()`. The comment says the runtime is "the engine own answer to can shipping code deliver this kind", which is correct and is exactly why it must be inverted when the answer changes.
  2. test_resolving_a_quest_only_source_answers_no_shipped_route (line 187) asserts the reason is `no_shipped_route` for an item whose only route is quest. That assertion becomes FALSE for the same reason, and it is not a bug in the test - a quest source that pays is no longer an unshipped kind.
  3. The unspent-grant test (lines 116-127) asserts `unspent.size() == 1`, that the unpaid grant names the sealed item, and that the inventory is BYTE-IDENTICAL afterwards. Once QuestGrants.pay delivers, the grant is paid, `unspent` is empty, and the inventory is not byte-identical - which is the whole point of the change.

So the quest edge is not a two-file change. It is quest_grants.gd + item_sources.gd + the flag, and then this test file has to be INVERTED rather than deleted: each of those three assertions encodes the old contract, and the correct new contract is the same three assertions pointed the other way (shipped, a satisfied-or-probed reason, a paid grant with a changed inventory). Deleting them would lose the criterion-5 and criterion-7 coverage that game/tests/acquisition exists to provide, and criterion 7 needs the REFUSAL half kept too - an item grant naming a definition that does not resolve must still come back unspent with a named reason.

The session delivering the edge does not own game/tests/acquisition, so it could not have seen this. Claimed separately (quest-test-contract) so nobody else picks the file up mid-flight.

title: QUEST EDGE LANDED RED: 9 failures + 2 aborted across 6 suites, masked by an import crash that --skip-import reveals
next:
THE EDGE LANDED RED, and the import failure was hiding it. Recorded by running the suite rather than by reading the diff, because for one turn the evidence said "shipped" and the run says otherwise.

THE IMPORT CRASH AND THE SUITE RESULT ARE SEPARATE. `tools test --suite quest` failed three times at the import step with exit 4294967295 and a 73-byte log, which is DEF-0143s signature. Removing 17 orphaned .uid files (DEF-0143s other named cause) did NOT fix it. What worked is the flag that already exists on the launcher: `tools test --skip-import`, which is safe once .godot/ is populated and which keeps every RAM, disk and clock ceiling. So DEF-0143s prescribed remedy - invoking the Godot binary directly to surface stderr - is unnecessary AND forbidden (INC-0004/0005: no ceilings at all, which is the shape behind the 73 GB run and the power-cycle). Correct that entry.

WHAT THE RUN SAYS: 625 passed, 9 failed across 6 suites, and 2 script errors that ABORTED a test mid-function, so the run itself says the count is a floor and "the run above is incomplete".

  test_quest_acquisition.gd      expected no_inventory_dependency       <- BL-0778 predicted this exactly
  test_quest.gd                  expected no_inventory_dependency, got unknown_item
  test_quest_content.gd          a fate gate on duels_won                <- unrelated to delivery
  test_quest_delivers_an_item.gd already_active: expected true, got false      <- the NEW suite, failing
  test_quest_screen.gd           5 failures, all already_active

THE `already_active` SHAPE IS THE CLUE, and it points AWAY from the delivery change. The same refusal appears in the new suite and in test_quest_screen.gd, across five assertions there ("a quest is now in flight: expected not true, got true", "the first press takes it on: expected true, got false", "the second is refused: expected false, got true"). A cascade that consistent is one cause, and it is not a grant that pays too much: `quest_def.gds` change in the same commit is DOCSTRING-ONLY (six lines describing the new item grant), so nothing in it can reject an accept.

The likeliest cause is CROSS-SUITE STATE rather than a product regression: the new suites setup calls QuestFixtureCatalog.teardown(), which loads the SHIPPED quest tree, so the test operates on real content and can inherit a quest already active in the shared process. That is consistent with the author note in the file itself - "which is exactly what made an earlier draft of this file report an unclaimed beat instead of its own mistake" - so fixture drift was already the known problem here. Stated as the leading hypothesis and NOT as a conclusion: distinguishing a real accept-path regression from cross-suite pollution needs a baseline run of these suites at the commit before 4daf0927, and that cannot be taken on this shared tree because the only way to get it is a checkout or a stash, both forbidden.

WHAT IS PROVEN AND WHAT IS NOT. Proven: the edge compiles, lints and formats clean; 625 assertions pass in the quest area; the two `no_inventory_dependency` failures are the old contract BL-0778 said must be inverted. Not proven: that the quest area is green. It is not, and the remaining work is a session that owns quest AND can iterate on a run - the two constraints that made this unfinishable in one pass.

title: WAVE 4: the quest route is LIVE - the gate is down to ONE gap from two, and the remainder is content
next:
THE QUEST ROUTE IS NOW LIVE, and the gate is down to ONE gap from two. Measured, not asserted:

    uv run python -m tools data audit --fail-on-unreachable
    fail 1697 item(s) declare a quest:<id> naming one of 442 quest ids no authored QuestDef defines
    fail data audit failed: 1 runtime-availability gap(s)
    delivered per live route: boss 1297, craft 323, domain 6362, gather 15, quest 1, starter 1

The gap that closed is "acquisition source quest has no shipping route". What it took was THREE declarations agreeing, which is the whole point of that finding:

  1. ItemSources.KINDS[KIND_QUEST].shipped flipped false -> true. This is the games own answer, and it was the LAST of the three, not the first: flipping it while delivery was still recording grants would have made 1697 items advertise a route that grants nothing, which is the ADR 0065 failure the file names for fates.
  2. A RUNTIME_ROUTES entry citing the production chain. The citation CANNOT be QuestApi.advance, because _route_module_dir excludes the declaring module and a module cannot vouch for itself - QuestBeatHandler calls advance from INSIDE quest. So it cites what app/ actually contains: world_pulse.gd registering the beat sink, and quest_program.gd:126, the one production caller of QuestApi.accept.
  3. A `kind == "quest"` membership branch in _runtime_roots, backed by _quest_granted_ids() reading the authored grants lists.

THE THIRD ONE EXPOSED A SECOND COPY INSIDE ONE FILE, which is the finding worth keeping. _runtime_roots and _route_roots_by_kind each implement the per-kind membership decision independently, with their own boss/starter/domain/gather branches. Adding quest to the first left the partition reporting `quest 0` and would have counted a quest-delivered item as NOT deliverable, because the second accumulates `outright` on its own. That is ADR 0066s second-copy failure with both copies in the same module, and it is invisible to the gate: the route is declared, called, and reported as delivering nothing. Recorded rather than refactored, because unifying the two is a real refactor of a file another session has been editing.

_quest_granted_ids() reads QUEST_DIR rather than a path of its own, deliberately: QUEST_DIR is the same tree _authored_quest_ids() resolves quest:<id> against, and a membership check reading a different tree than the reference check would let an item count as quest-deliverable while its quest:<id> still read as dangling.

WHAT THE REMAINING GAP IS, and it is not code. 1697 items name one of 442 quest ids that no authored QuestDef defines. Closing it means authoring 442 quests or repairing 1697 source lines in game/data/, which this session does not own. It is content, it was content before the route went live, and no code change moves it - the gate says so rather than counting it as fixed. Note the shape: authoring quests that grant items is the ONLY way an item joins _quest_granted_ids(), so that content work is also what makes the route worth more than the single item it is worth today.

Also noted, and NOT fixed because it belongs to another session: game/src/modules/loot/loot_content_tables.gd is untracked and its Parse Errors ("the member PROFILE_FIELDS already exists in parent class LootContentRecords", and AFFLICTION_FIELD and MAX_NESTING_DEPTH likewise) make `tools test` exit 1 even when every suite passes. It is a mid-refactor parse error in loot, unrelated to quest, and recorded here rather than touched.
